opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is one of the most overlooked questions in the field right now. We've become very focused on the loss number. If the loss goes down and the benchmark goes up, we assume the model is good. But two systems can produce exactly the same outputs on the training data and be completely different inside. And that internal difference matters enormously for what happens next.

What got me thinking about this was Picbreeder, the old interactive evolution experiment where people bred images. When you look inside the networks that produced some of those images, like a skull or an apple, you see something remarkable. The representation is beautifully organized. There's a part of the network that corresponds to symmetry, and if you change that one weight you get a symmetric change, like the mouth opening. It's modular in a way that reflects the actual structure of the thing. We started calling that a unified factored representation.

Then if you take the same image and train a network to reproduce it with SGD, conventionally, you get the same output pixel for pixel. Same loss, essentially perfect. But inside it's a mess. Things that should be one concept are split up and duplicated in different places, and things that should be separate are tangled together. We call that fractured entangled representation. From the outside you'd never know. The output looks identical.

The reason I care is that the representation determines what the system can do beyond the training task. It affects how it generalizes, how creative it can be, how well it can keep learning, and whether it can come up with genuinely new ideas. If the underlying structure is fractured, you might get there by memorizing a huge patchwork of special cases, and that can look great on benchmarks while being brittle in ways that are hard to see. You see hints of this in large models that can do something sophisticated and then fail at a trivially related variation.

So the loss tells you that you got to the destination, but not how you got there, and the "how" is what determines where you can go next. That connects to everything I've thought about with open-endedness and why greatness cannot be planned. In Picbreeder, nobody was trying to make a skull. The good representations came out of a process that wasn't driven by a single objective, where people were building stepping stones on stepping stones. That kind of history seems to lay down a deeply structured representation, while hammering directly at an objective tends to get you there by whatever hack works.

I'm not saying SGD is bad or that big models aren't impressive. They clearly are. But if we only measure output performance, we're blind to something important, and that matters if we want systems that are creative and can keep building on what they know.

r001.rationale: The response says representation affects how a model generalizes and warns that brittle systems may look good on benchmarks while failing on related variations.

r002.rationale: It lists downstream capabilities and says output performance leaves important information unseen, but does not state that those capabilities are harder to quantify than training loss.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the loss tells you what the network achieved, not how it achieved it, and the "how" is what determines everything that happens next. Two networks can hit essentially identical loss on the same task and be completely different inside. One has found a modular, factored representation where the regularities of the problem are captured by a small number of components that each mean something, and the other has stitched together a patchwork of special cases that happens to cover the training distribution. From the outside, from the loss alone, they look the same. But if you want to fine-tune them, or ask them to generalize, or build on top of them, or just understand what they learned, they behave completely differently.

This is what we were seeing in the fractured entangled representation work. We took the picturebreeder networks, which were evolved through this open-ended, human-guided search process, and compared them with networks trained by SGD to produce the exact same images. Same output, same task, same objective, basically same performance. And when you look inside, the SGD-trained networks are a mess. The concept of symmetry, which is visually obvious in the image, isn't anywhere in the network as a unit. It's smeared across the weights, entangled with everything else. In the evolved networks you can find a single node that controls symmetry, and you can sweep it and watch the symmetry change while everything else stays intact. That's a representation that knows something, in a way the fractured one doesn't, even though both drew the same picture.

So I think the loss is deceptive as a measure of understanding. It's a measure of coverage. It tells you the function was approximated on the data you had, and it's silent on whether the approximation is built out of the right parts. We've gotten very good at driving loss down, and I think we've fooled ourselves into believing that implies something about the quality of what's inside, when actually the whole theory of why generalization and creativity and continual learning should come out of that is pretty thin. What I care about is whether the model has carved the problem at its joints, and the loss just can't see that.

r001.rationale: The response says the networks behave differently when asked to generalize and contrasts a representation that captures regularities with one that only covers the training distribution.

r002.rationale: The response says training loss does not reveal a model’s internal representation or downstream behavior, but it does not clearly state that desired downstream capabilities are harder to quantify than training loss.

astra-6.text:
Because the training loss doesn’t tell you what the model actually discovered. Two models can get the same score and yet solve the problem in very different ways. One might have discovered something general, and the other might have found a shortcut that only works in the particular circumstances we gave it. Those differences become important when you ask it to do something new.

And there’s a deeper issue here that interests me, which is that solving the task we set isn’t necessarily the most interesting thing that can come out of learning. Sometimes a system discovers a representation or a behavior that becomes a stepping stone to something else. It might not even improve the score on the current task, but it opens up possibilities that weren’t there before.

So if we look only at the loss, we’re treating everything about the solution as interchangeable except its performance on this one objective. But from the perspective of discovery, those solutions aren’t interchangeable at all. How you got there determines where you can go next.

r001.rationale: It contrasts general solutions with shortcuts that work only in the given circumstances, and says those differences matter when the model faces something new.

r002.rationale: It says training loss misses representations, behaviors, and future possibilities, but does not clearly state that the downstream capabilities people ultimately want are harder to quantify than the loss.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, because the training loss doesn’t tell you what the system has actually discovered. You can have two systems that perform equally well on a task, but one has discovered something much more general, while the other has found a trick that only works in that particular setting. And those are very different outcomes, even if the objective function can’t distinguish them.

This becomes especially important if you think of that solution as a stepping stone. What does it make possible next? A solution that looks inefficient or unnecessarily complicated for the current task might contain the beginnings of an ability that becomes incredibly useful later. If you only care about getting the lowest loss right now, you have no particular reason to preserve that.

So I care about how it solves the task because the task isn’t necessarily the end of the story. The interesting question is what kind of foundation you’re creating for further discovery, and that’s not captured by a single performance number.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a general solution with a trick that works only in a particular setting, communicating that the way the model solves the task affects generalization.

r002.rationale: It says future useful abilities and the foundation for further discovery are not captured by a single performance number, conveying that downstream capabilities are harder to assess than training loss.
